newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Record trade deficit haunts S.Korea's economy.
newsitem.headline: Record trade deficit haunts S.Korea's economy.

text.p: Labour strife and plunging chip prices, the main culprits behind a record trade deficit in January, have set up South Korea's economy for a depressing start to the lunar new year.
Economists said at the weekend the fallout from Hanbo Steel Co's financial failure would add more gloom to an already overcast business climate.
The trade ministry said on Saturday the trade deficit widened to $3.48 billion in January from $2.13 billion a year ago.
"This is the largest monthly trade deficit in Korea's history," a senior ministry official said.
A sharp drop in semiconductor exports, the largest export item, was largely responsible for the huge shortfall, the ministry said.
Semiconductor sales abroad plunged 44.2 percent in January due to a fall in chip prices. Exports excluding computer chips rose 2.0 percent.
The price of a 16 megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chip, which is used to make personal computers, fell to $8 last month from $43 a year ago.
The ministry also blamed more than three weeks of wildcat stries for the record deficit.

The labour unrest, which has cost the country hundreds of millions of dollars in lost exports, began on December 26 when the ruling party rammed a new labour law through parliament to make it easier for companies to sack workers and replace strikers.

The automobile industry was hit hardest, with an output loss totalling 2.39 trillion won ($2.77 billion) and an export loss put at $369.9 million. The strikes also cut ship exports by $51.4 million and electronic parts shipments by $29.8 million.
"If not for the strikes, exports excluding semiconductors would have risen 6.1 percent," a ministry statement said.

Economists said steel exports were also flagging because of the insolvency of Hanbo Steel, the nation's second largest steelmaker. A decline in steel output could hit the automobile, machinery and shipbuilding industries further.
Hanbo defaulted on debt repayments on January 23 after accumulating five trillion won in loans.
Analysts warned that the Hanbo crisis could lead to a rise in interest rates and push some smaller companies to the wall by making it difficult for them to obtain loans.
The ministry said it expected the trade deficit to narrow to $14 billion for the whole of 1997 from $20.38 billion last year.
"The trade balance is expected to improve in the near future as the labour unrest eases and companies operate longer hours to make up for lost exports," the ministry official said.
But economists said January's deficit represented a quarter of the annual target and that the yen's fall versus the dollar would continue to hit exports.
The yen's weakness would make low-end Japanese products more competitive against South Korean goods.
"The government would feel a lot of pressure to meet the trade target," said Lee Geun-tae, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute.
Some economists said the government might launch an austerity campaign to fight the ballooning deficit.

"The government could force oil companies to reduce oil purchases and ask chaebols (conglomerates) to cut back on imports of consumer goods," said Shin Hoo-shik, an economist at Daewoo Economic Research Institute.
"But that's not going to be easy."
